items.title: Van Rysel Drops Weight and Adds Aero to the New RCR-R Lineup
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Developed directly with the Decathlon CMA CGM WorldTour team, the second-generation RCR-R platform drops weight and blends lessons from the dedicated aero bike.
items.lbText:
Today Van Rysel is launching a new version of the RCR-R and RCR-R PRO all-around race bikes. This is a continuation of the work that started when Van Rysel, Decathlon’s in-house performance cycling brand, sprang to life in Lille, France, in 2019. The brand then really catapulted into the global spotlight when it took over as the bike sponsor for the Decathlon CMA CGM WorldTour team in 2024.

As part of that sponsorship, Van Rysel splits its lineup between the RCR-F dedicated aero platform and the RCR as a lightweight generalist. Today’s launch is an attempt to bring what Van Rysel learned from the dedicated aero platform into the generalist racing chassis while dropping weight.

While Van Rysel is part of the larger Decathlon organization, the team has historically operated like a much more nimble brand. Part of that agility is evident in the relatively short development cycle we are seeing here. According to the brand, this new platform is the result of a mere two-and-a-half-year turnaround, driven heavily by direct feedback from the Decathlon CMA CGM team.

To land on the final shape, Van Rysel worked through a claimed 13 CFD iterations, five wind-tunnel prototypes, and seven different carbon layups. The stated goal was to find the sweet spot between the aerodynamics of the dedicated RCR-F PRO and the feel of a lightweight climbing bike. To pull that off, the company essentially tried to split the difference across the chassis. By marrying a rigid front end for aerodynamic power transfer with a rear triangle that allows for controlled flex, Van Rysel claims the design mimics the traction and high-speed descending stability of a dedicated climber without sacrificing the speed of an aero rig.

Van Rysel also worked aerodynamic bottles and cages into the overall design. This approach is not unlike what we have seen from Trek and Enve, and the reasoning is obvious: it provides free aero gains with virtually no downside, provided it is executed well. Unfortunately, we won’t know how well it works right away. The images shared only show standard bottles, and Van Rysel notes that “the aero bottles will be released separately from the bikes, with further details to follow.” Despite the delay, the brand claims that in testing featuring turbulence and pedaling legs, the proprietary bottle setup saves up to 6.3 watts at 45 km/h (28 mph) over the previous generation.

Ultimately, both the PRO and the standard model share the exact same silhouette and geometry. They differ only in their carbon fiber layups and component build options, though both frames reportedly utilize the identical 360-gram fork.

At the top of the hierarchy sits the RCR-R PRO. To drop the weight on this tier, Van Rysel relies on a specific blend of super-high-modulus and high-modulus carbon fiber. According to the brand, this layup brings a size medium frame down to 705 grams, making it the lightest chassis the company has ever produced. On the scale, that translates to a claimed complete bike weight of 6.6 kg (14.5 lbs) for the flagship SRAM RED AXS build. For component options, the PRO tier is offered in four configurations: Shimano Dura-Ace Di2, Shimano Ultegra Di2, SRAM RED AXS, and SRAM Force AXS.

Sitting below the flagship model is the standard RCR-R, aimed at riders wanting the new chassis at a more accessible price point. While it uses the same aerodynamic mold as the PRO, Van Rysel relies on a standard high-modulus carbon layup for this tier. That shift in material adds a bit of mass, pushing the claimed frame weight up to 883 grams. On the complete bike side, the Ultegra Di2 build is the lightest configuration offered, tipping the scales at a claimed 7.4 kg (16.3 lbs). To keep costs down, the brand is speccing this frame exclusively with mid-to-upper-tier electronic groupsets, giving buyers the choice of Shimano 105 Di2 or Ultegra Di2, as well as SRAM Rival AXS or Force AXS.

While Van Rysel pulled the cover off the new bikes today at Rouleur Live in London, they won’t be hitting showroom floors immediately. Commercial availability is slated to open after the new year on January 5, 2027. When they do go on sale, European pricing will range from €3,299 up to €8,499 depending on the chosen frame tier and component build. For more details on the new lineup, visit the Van Rysel website .

items.title: Matthew Richardson Allegedly Targeted Teammate With Offensive Images in Track Worlds Scandal
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Richardson sent home from Shanghai in disgrace after reportedly using homophobic and racist slurs as British Cycling is rocked by allegations of 'toxic culture.'
items.lbText:
(Photo: Dilara Irem Sancar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Matthew Richardson was sent home from the UCI track world championships last month in disgrace after he allegedly targeted a teammate with offensive images.

That’s the new detail The Times reported Tuesday on a scandal that’s rocked the small world of track cycling.

The Times wrote that Richardson – one of the best sprinters of his era – had left a long regular trail of homophobic and discriminatory remarks about people from minority backgrounds.

One of those was made in a message that included “a deeply offensive image with reference to another Team GB rider.”

The image sparked an allegation being made against Richardson.

The complaint saw him sent home from Shanghai by British Cycling on the eve of October’s UCI track worlds.

“The Times has seen extensive evidence, dating back over a number of years, of images and messages sent by Richardson to other riders. He appears to make discriminatory remarks about people from minority backgrounds on a regular basis,” reads the report.

“The Times has seen six different messages where he appears to use the racially offensive n-word, and others where he jokes about his use of that word. He also appears to have made a number of offensive references to the Asian community and homophobic comments. Another senior source claims to have seen a separate image, again sent to riders, that references a rider from another international team and uses the n-word.”

Richardson was born in England but moved to Australia as a child.

He switched racing nationality from Australian to English in 2024.

British Cycling confirmed it opened an investigation into Richardson’s conduct after he was axed from its world championship squad.

The 27-year-old vowed he would fully co-operate in the proceedings “with contrition.”

However, according to The Times, the allegations against Richardson dated back to July – three months before the investigation was opened. Additionally, Richardson was only withdrawn 48 hours before the world championships in Shanghai last month.

These developments come at a difficult time for British Cycling.

In a separate thread, The Times reported that an independent feedback survey of the federation uncovered a drop in morale among elite riders, a lack of accountability in senior leadership, and accusations of a “toxic culture.”

Richardson’s agent has distanced himself from the rider in the wake of the allegations against the rider.

However, Richardson is still headlining the London 3-Day track cycling event this weekend. The event is not affiliated to British Cycling.

British Cycling has not provided any timelines on the conclusion of its investigation.

items.title: MET’s New Manta 3 Aero Helmet Promises 6 Free Watts. Here Is What the Data Actually Says.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: The Italian brand finally details the tech behind Tadej Pogačar’s WorldTour helmet. We break down the F1-inspired aero claims, the 250-gram footprint, and why its 5-star safety rating matters more than ever.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Sprintcyclingagency/MET helmets)

Today, MET is officially taking the wraps off the MET Manta 3. However, if you’ve been paying attention to the WorldTour, you have actually been looking at this helmet since March. Tadej Pogačar and UAE Team Emirates quietly debuted the new design at Milano-Sanremo, and it has been a frequent sight at the front of the peloton ever since. Now, the Italian brand is officially launching this update to its aero-focused race helmet.

For many, the MET Manta was as much about UAE Team Emirates wins as anything standout with the helmet itself. The previous version used the much older MIPS with the familiar yellow insert, and independent testing never showed it as a standout, instead placing it among less aero-specific helmets like the Specialized Propero. It is also not hard to see that the previous design relied heavily on minimal front vents to get what aero advantage it did have.

The team at MET claims to have attacked each of those deficits in the new helmet. According to the brand, the Manta 3 provides a 6-watt aerodynamic advantage over the previous generation. To get there, MET relied on extensive wind-tunnel testing and full-scale rider modeling. Of course, that data does not come with a speed claim to match, so it is highly likely that number was generated at 50 km/h, where a full 6 watts is still impressive but not quite as groundbreaking. Either way, it likely puts the new helmet into the upper echelon of the fastest road helmets.

To achieve that, MET used what it refers to as a “Double Deck” rear architecture. That means an F1-inspired rear tail that MET claims smooths airflow in aggressive riding positions while simultaneously aiding heat dissipation. It also happens to look much like the add-on UFO (Unidentified Fast Object) that Limar featured on the Air Atlas launched in 2022 and later updated to the Air Atlas UAP in early 2026. Both designs borrow on the principles of long-tail TT helmets, but keeping the tail shorter is likely better for real-world usability across different body shapes and head positions.

Aerodynamics is only one part of this design change, though. The idea of the “Double Deck” architecture is to speed up airflow through the helmet as well as smooth the join to the upper back. When that works in any helmet, it creates a low-pressure zone at the rear that sucks hot air out of the inside while simultaneously speeding the flow across the scalp. You can also see there is more front-facing ventilation, and the yellow MIPS liner is gone in favor of the modern, minimalist Mips Air Node Pro rotational impact protection system integrated into the Coolmax padding.

While it feels like almost every premium helmet boasts a 5-star Virginia Tech rating these days, the reality is a bit more nuanced. The lab essentially scores on a curve; as helmet technology across the industry improves, a helmet has to perform objectively better just to earn that top mark. MET managing to hit that shifting 5-star standard puts the Manta 3 in elite company. If you look across the current aero helmet market, popular options like the Giant Pursuit, Giro Eclipse Pro, Sweet Protection Tucker III 2vi, Mavic Comete Ultimate, and Kask Nirvana haven’t even been run through the lab’s protocol, while heavy-hitting premium competitors like the Specialized S-Works Evade 4 and the Trek Ballista MIPS currently sit at 4-star ratings.

To get there, MET took a genuinely interesting approach to its underlying safety development. The company collected and analyzed 142 crashed helmets pulled directly from UAE Team Emirates riders between 2019 and 2025. By comparing the structural damage from those real-world WorldTour wrecks against standardized lab metrics, MET says it crash-tested over 250 physical samples of the new Manta 3—totaling more than 745 individual impacts—to fine-tune the energy dissipation of the EPS liner. That optimized foam structure works in tandem with the Mips Air Node Pro system mentioned above, handling rotational impact management without the bulk of a traditional plastic slip-plane.

Just like a bike frame, prioritizing aerodynamics in a helmet usually comes with a weight penalty. However, 250 grams is right at the sweet spot for a good aero helmet, and MET managed to hit that number with a CE-certified size medium Manta 3. To keep the helmet durable at that weight, the brand opted for a full-wrap construction. By using 10 individual polycarbonate shells to completely enclose the raw EPS foam, the design protects the vulnerable lower edges from daily dings and travel wear. Finally, fit is handled by the Safe-T Orbital system, which offers standard vertical, occipital, and circumferential adjustments, alongside dedicated side vents that do double-duty as secure sunglass ports.

The MET Manta 3 officially launches today, November 12, with commercial availability rolling out throughout the month. Retail pricing is set at $375, €330, and £299.99. For more information visit the MET website .

items.title: Sepp Kuss Eats Cookies for Breakfast and Is Embarrassed by Trophies. He’s Pro Cycling’s Hero Next Door.
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: New documentary reveals how the US star found balance in the rigorous world of pro bike racing. The answer? Be reassuringly normal.
items.lbText:
(Photo: OSCAR DEL POZO/AFP via Getty Images)

Sepp Kuss could just be the dude next door who’s good at riding bikes.

In a new “Day in the Life” video, Kuss walks viewers through the boring mundanity of his life at home in Andorra during the off-season.

As you’d expect from Colorado’s fan favorite, it’s all pretty chill.

There are cookies for breakfast, grand tour trophies gathering dust in hallways, and a man-cave cluttered with bike bits.

His lifestyle seems hilariously lackadaisical. His home has few trappings of an elite athlete who’s likely getting paid seven figures.

The high-end Porsche parked in the garage is the one giveaway that this is not your normal guy.

Visma-Lease a Bike released its “Day in the Life” mini-doc this week after its long-signed American star blasted through one of his best seasons yet.

This year, Kuss rode all three grand tours in the season for the second time in his career.

The “Eagle of Durango” won a stage at the Giro d’Italia, nearly won two stages at the Tour de France, and made a late surge for fifth overall at the Vuelta a España.

Few riders dare take on three grand tours in a season, but Kuss made it look easy.

In the video, Kuss says the program keeps life how he likes it – simple and stress-free.

“I’ve been able to be home a lot between all three grand tours [this year], and that makes a big difference,” he says.

“Mentally it was easier than a normal season, because you have really concrete blocks and concrete goals. Between that, it’s a pretty simple routine and easy living,” he says.

Kuss’ young family is no doubt front of mind when he structures his calendar.

His Spanish-born wife, Noemi, and two-year-old daughter, Martina, feature heavily in the documentary, and Sepp is in all-out dad-mode throughout.

He plays with his daughter, takes her on a bike ride, and helps Noemi feed her bits of cake.

Kuss is pro cycling’s ultimate dad next door.

He’s just a 32-year-old dude who casually enjoys bikes, baking, and crushing Tour de France climbs at a billion watts per kilo.

And yes, you read that right, Kuss appears to be a passionate baker – one with a sweet tooth.

Food and food-prep feature heavily in the show.

There’s no controversial kimchi-and-gnocchi concoction like the one favored by Matteo Jorgenson, but there are some interesting insights.

Kuss reveals a refreshingly casual attitude to food that’s careful but far from restrictive.

“Every morning has to start with cookies or a cake,” Kuss says as he cuts the final slices of what looks like a huge home bake.

“We usually try to go for something more homemade, but a lot of the time it’s just normal cookies from the grocery store. Not a perfect diet,” he smiles.

The waifish climber adds that he barely restricts and allows a little luxury, all year round.

It’s no doubt all carefully considered and meticulously tracked on a food app, but Kuss doesn’t appear overly concerned about optimizing his W/Kg ratio in the depths of off-season.

“My diet is never so strict. It stays pretty much the same all year,” he says. “We eat well, but there’s nothing that I don’t eat in the off-season versus in the normal season.

“There are always some chips in the pantry,” he adds.

Kuss’s “aww shucks” character and boyish charm have made him one of the darlings of the pro peloton.

He’s well liked by his colleagues, loved by the media (he’ll rarely say no to an interview), and adored by fans.

Kuss’ reluctant stardom is epitomized as the camera follows him through his home.

Bike mementos are casually scattered in random places and seemingly displayed out of obligation.

The huge wine bottle he won at the Giro d’Italia is gathering dust in a doorway.

His Vuelta a España stage-winner’s plaque sits on a shelf in the garage alongside a handmade #GCKuss token and a bunch of random bike oils.

“You either have a trophy room, or you find the nice ones to put somewhere, but …,” Kuss says with a shy shrug.

Kuss’ garage also functions as a bike store and workshop.

Unlike the many pros who can barely change a tire, Kuss is teaching himself the art of bike maintenance as a “hobby mechanic.”

Oh, and the special-edition red Cervélo that Kuss rode on the final stage of his career-crowning ride at the Vuelta?

Lost in a mess of a half-dozen bikes hanging in a rack.

What did you expect? A pride-of-place position hanging on the wall of his lounge?

Kuss is one of the greatest U.S. racers of his generation.

He became the first North American to win a grand tour in a decade when he won the 2023 Vuelta a España, and is one of the few active pros to have taken a stage at all three of cycling’s three-week races.

But Kuss often seems embarrassed by his own success.

It should be considered a miracle then, that his Vuelta a España winner’s trophy has made it out of the cupboard.

The large circular prize he was awarded in 2023 stands on a cabinet in a dark corner of his home.

And that low-key position should be considered progress.

Last year, Kuss revealed in a Sigma Sport video that his prestigious trophy wasn’t proudly standing triumphant in a cabinet, but tucked deep in the back of a cupboard.

Visma’s recently retired Dutch stalwart Robert Gesink makes a cameo appearance in the video when he meets Kuss for a coffee.

The 40-year-old believes Kuss’ innate zen has bought him longevity.

“The biggest strength of Sepp is that he found the really nice balance,” Gesink says. “He does everything right, he weighs his food, he does his training correctly, but he has the right balance and doesn’t overdo it.

“If you can keep that balance and find a way that works for you and you can sustain that level, then you can keep growing,” Gesink continues.

“That’s how you can build such a long and successful career if you find your own way to make that sustainable and not lose yourself straight away in all these little details.”

Kuss is currently out in L.A. visiting Cervélo HQ with several Visma-Lease a Bike teammates.…

items.title: The Best Shoe Covers I’ve Ever Used Are 55% Off and Even Cheaper Than Last Year
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: The Specialized Neoprene shoe covers are so good I stopped using winter boots—and right now, they’ve never been cheaper.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The vast majority of cycling shoe covers aren’t that good. Most of them don’t work, and even if they do kind of work, they rip if you look at them wrong—and usually cost a fortune. The Specialized Neoprene shoe covers are the best I’ve ever used.

I keep thinking they are about to go off the market, but so far they just keep dropping in price. If you ever ride in the rain and cold, these have actually replaced my winter boots, and right now they’ve never been cheaper.

There are two main problems with most shoe covers, and Specialized solves them both. The first is that getting shoe covers on is usually such a hassle that half the time you just chance the weather rather than bothering with the struggle. On that front, these don’t have zippers, aren’t crazy tight, and the Velcro closure at the bottom is easy. The trickiest part is getting your bib tight situated above the upper cuff without wrinkling, but the thickness of the material helps there.

That tall upper solves the second problem. Shoe covers don’t generally leak through the material; instead, water seeps in from above the cuff. Specialized starts to fix that by adding height to the cuff, but that’s not enough on its own.

Your bib tights will leak if you ride long enough in the rain. A pair of hardshell rain pants will solve this, but if you aren’t wearing them, you need the best possible seal you can get at the ankle. Specialized uses a strip of silicone to help keep water from running down your leg and into your shoe. Add some VeloToze waterproof cuffs , and you can keep your feet dry with just bib tights and shoe covers alone.

items.title: The Argon 18 Anti Matter Is Just a Road Bike With Huge Tires. Half of You Will Hate It.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Depending on your gravel priorities, the unapologetically aero Argon 18 Anti Matter is either a rigid nightmare or the ultimate race weapon. Where do you fall?
items.lbText:
Aero focused Co-developed Apidura aero bags included Zipp wheels/Power Meter at both the Force and RED level Available as a chassis only 55mm tire clearance

While the Factor Sarana is the bike that got the overall nod at our Future of Gravel Field Test , the Argon 18 Anti Matter—or perhaps the newly released Factor Elara—is likely the bike I’d prefer for my own personal gravel riding. I also happen to see this approach as the future of the sport far more than an endurance race bike.

The problem is that my reasoning relies on a few assumptions that might be up for debate. I believe fewer people ride truly rough gravel compared to those who spend their time on relatively smooth dirt roads and the tarmac required to get there. I’m not sure if everyone will agree with that, but my other assumption—or perhaps bias is a better word—is that most people prioritize going fast.

As long as those assumptions hold true, aero gravel is clearly the future. Smoother roads mean fewer technical demands and higher average speeds. That means aerodynamics play a much bigger part, and since people like going fast, prioritizing aero makes sense. Of course, I also love a bike like this for its long-distance efficiency; I would absolutely pick the Anti Matter if I were doing the Traka 360 a second time, and it doubles as a highly capable road option.

The reason this bike ultimately didn’t win our field test is that, at least for now, it remains a somewhat specialty machine. You have to really want speed, and you have to be willing to deal with the extra stiffness and weight to unlock those advantages—not that a 950g frameset is particularly heavy. Still, it might be exactly the right tool for you. Let’s get into what I like, and what I don’t, about the Argon 18 Anti Matter.

It’s the speed! I like free speed, and it makes no sense to me that everyone doesn’t share the same opinion. Argon 18 claims that the Anti Matter is 14.5 watts faster at 45 km/h than the brand’s round-tube gravel race bike, the Dark Matter. Aerodynamically speaking, I’d guess the Dark Matter is fairly similar to the Giant we tested during this series, making the Giant a perfect stand-in to represent a standard, non-aero gravel frame. Most of the crew loved that bike because it’s so light, but personally, I’ll take the free speed.

Of course, we have to acknowledge the caveat in that math: most people aren’t riding gravel at 45 km/h (28 mph). But even if we shrink that speed down to 18 mph—a very doable pace for most people on fast gravel—the Anti Matter still saves you 3.9 watts. Now, if you read that and think, “Who cares about 4 watts? That’s nothing!” think about what it would mean the next time you are completing a VO2 max interval if it were 4 watts easier. Maybe initially you don’t care, but as those sets run longer, I bet you’d be pretty happy to have that energy back.

I also like to look at it over time. Let’s say you are looking to ride Unbound 200. You are a regular person, like me, and you aren’t competing for a podium, but you are out there for 14 to 20 hours. Those 4 watts sound insignificant until you multiply them by 15 hours. I don’t expect to use aero to win a town sign sprint. Instead, I am adding up those frame watts saved along with the much larger gains of an aero riding position, an aero helmet, the right clothes, and an aero wheelset. Just like scrutinizing every gram, pretty soon that tiny 4-watt frame advantage becomes a total system savings of 20 to 30 watts. Over a 15-hour day in the Flint Hills, that translates to banking energy and shaving upwards of 30 to 45 minutes off your total time. I don’t care that I am not all that fast; I am pulling free watts where I can, and everything matters.

What I also like about this bike is that the team at Argon 18 is as obsessive as I am. The bike includes Apidura aero frame bags that are both highly functional and aerodynamically improve the frame. There are aero bottle cages that load from the side, so you can run full-size bottles with the frame bag mounted. The aero handlebar also features a good out-front mount. And on top of it all, you aren’t asked to downsize your tires. The frame will fit a 55mm tire, so you can plow through the rough stuff at whatever speed you are riding.

As much as I don’t like to admit it, the aerodynamics aren’t completely free speed. Closing the gap between the front tire and the downtube is aerodynamically faster, but pulling that wheel in requires a steeper head tube angle and a shorter front center. The trade-off is that the bike feels noticeably less stable when the gravel gets truly rough. While a bike like the Factor Sarana wants to comfortably plow straight ahead, the Anti Matter demands your constant attention and can feel nervous on high-speed, chunky descents.

Then there is the toe overlap. As someone who rides size 54 frames and spends a lot of time on the road, almost every bike I’ve ever owned has had some degree of toe overlap. On the road, it rarely matters because you lean to turn. Put this bike on technical gravel, though, and it matters a lot. Turning around a tight switchback at low speed becomes a whole choreographed event. I can even rub my toe on the tire just making quick steering adjustments to dodge rocks on a relatively straight, steep climb. It adds a frustrating cognitive load to technical sections because you constantly have to manage and time your pedal strokes with your steering.…

items.title: ‘Seixas Is Better Than Pogačar Was at That Age’: Geraint Thomas Overlooks the Pizza and PlayStation Factor
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: 'He just seems more advanced, more developed.' Geraint Thomas has a radical theory, but is it fair to compare Seixas and Pogačar like-for-like?
items.lbText:
It might be true, but the argument has got a flaw.

Speaking on the latest episode of his Watts Occurring podcast, Thomas drew the popular comparison between Paul Seixas and Tadej Pogačar .

The team Ineos long-timer and former Tour de France winner felt there’s only one winner, and he’s French.

“It was unreal from him this year. Fair play,” Thomas said of Seixas. “What can you say?

“He’s better than Pog when Pog was that age,” Thomas said. “It’s not just the wins, but how he seems. He just seems more advanced, more developed.”

Seixas has been spoken of with the reverence typically reserved for Pogačar throughout his incredible breakout season.

The spindly Frenchman tore apart Itzulia Basque Country and La Fléche Wallonne. He finished fourth at the Tour de France as a debuting 19-year-old. He became the youngest winner of Il Lombardia at age 20.

Thomas was adamant when speaking to Luke Rowe – who works as sport director on Seixas’ team at Decathlon CMA-CGM – that 2026 marked the arrival of cycling’s next dominator.

“It’s going to be an exciting few years for him and for France and for your team. He’s just going to continue to improve,” Thomas said.

Cycling hasn’t seen such a prodigious talent since the arrival of … well, Pogačar. They’re two phenoms, seven years apart.

But is it fair to draw parallels between their careers?

Pogačar’s countryman and long-time teammate Domen Novak would argue “no.”

Speaking earlier this March with Sportal , Novak highlighted an important distinction between the two: their teenage regimens.

“The guy is really very good,” Novak said of Seixas. ‘Everyone compares him to Tadej; they want to put him next to him, and considering his age, he is even better than Tadej was.

“But you need to know something else,” Novak told Sportal . “As far as I know Tadej, he didn’t do any altitude training in those early years. He was racing for the Gusto Ljubljana team. I can say that he won his first Tour while eating pizza, drinking beer and playing PlayStation.”

Novak was likely pouring on the hyperbole, but he has a point.

Seixas only turned 20 in September, but is already one of the most buttoned-down, hyper-professional athletes in the entire peloton.

He locked himself into a high-altitude training camp away from family and friends for two months in the winter, pulled a ridiculous three-week block to prepare for the Tour, and berates himself for every rookie racing error.

He’s got high standards and higher expectations.

There’s no doubt that his life is ruled by bathroom scales, HRV scores, and watt-per-kilo targets.

By contrast, 20-year-old Pogačar carried puppy fat and unabashed naiveté into his debut year with UAE Emirates-XRG.

In 2019, high-carb fueling and HRV tracking were pipedreams and disc brakes were for revolutionaries.

Not that such Stone Age approaches stopped Pogačar from winning the Tour of California and blasting to third on his grand tour debut at the Vuelta a España, of course.

Novak questioned the sustainability of Seixas’ approach when he spoke with Sportal . We won’t find out if his fears are well-founded for a decade.

Meanwhile, Thomas said on his podcast that only burnout or boredom will slow Pogačar’s stampede across pro cycling.

“Pog’s still improving. He was the best Pog this year than he has been,” Thomas said, caveating that the 28-year-old Pogačar of 2026 is without doubt better than the 20-year-old Seixas.

“He’s unique, don’t get me wrong, Pog,” Thomas continued.

“Mentally, if he can still commit and do everything right, he can keep improving until he’s 35,” he said.

If Thomas is right and Seixas and Pogačar both keep improving, we could have another seven years to argue over how they compare.

items.title: The One Metric Cyclists Over 40 Need to Start Watching
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: In your 20s and 30s, you could ride hard every day and recover overnight. But after 40 you need to start paying attention to a new metric if you want to avoid burnout and fatigue.
items.lbText:
When I was in my 30s—not even my 20s—I could finish a hard ride, hydrate with a couple of beers, refuel with a pizza, and do it all again the next day. I didn’t think a ton about training in general because it was easy. If I wanted to ride faster, I rode more, and I got faster more or less no matter what I did. I even went through a long phase of severely underfueling; I weighed nothing, yet I continued to get faster. Then things changed.

The first place I really noticed it was when I transitioned from outdoor summer riding to indoor winter training. When that happens, I shift from endurance to intensity, and I used to just shrug it off. Surely if I could handle a six-hour outdoor ride on a Sunday, a three-hour indoor ride would be easier, no matter the intensity. Except my mid-week VO2 max workouts suddenly seemed awfully hard, and if I jumped into a Zwift race, it was all I could do just to hold on. Then that same three-hour ride the next Sunday felt awful. Pretty soon I almost dreaded getting on the bike, finding myself dragging to the saddle each evening for whatever workout I had.

The change was aging. One of the more fascinating things about testosterone as a performance-enhancing drug in endurance sports is that it isn’t just about building muscle. It works for performance because it allows you to recover faster and absorb more hard workouts. Guess what falls as you age? Both men and women experience hormonal changes as a result of aging, and reduced recovery capacity is just one side effect. There are plenty of other biological changes, and they all add up to a single reality: you have to start paying attention to a new metric you might never have considered before.

For younger riders, modern cycling technology—head units, smartwatches, and power meters—acts as an accelerator. It is a tool used to chase maximum power output, hunt Strava segments, and push deeper into the red. But to survive and thrive in your 40s, you have to flip that. To keep pinning on numbers and exploring remote gravel roads, your technology must become your brake.

Look, I’m a tech guy. I like “cool” technology and I had smartwatches pretty early on. At some point, I moved to Garmin watches primarily, but I continued to test Google Pixel watches, and for the Apple folks out there, Apple Watches have always been great options. Through most of that journey, though, I wasn’t doing much with those devices. Recovery metrics weren’t important to me because I tracked my on-the-bike performance with my bike computer.

I wore a smartwatch for occasionally tracking a run and because I enjoyed the smart capabilities. Who cares what happened off the bike? I’d ignore the advice to limit Zwift racing because it was fun. If I did three races in a week and sometimes saw my Garmin report that my HRV was unbalanced, I wouldn’t be concerned. But as I got older, I started noticing a pattern. On the days my Garmin told me my Heart Rate Variability (HRV) was unbalanced, my workouts felt terrible.

For a lot of people, HRV sounds very abstract. It also seems like something that just happens to you. In reality, it’s your body’s “check engine” light. It measures the microscopic variations in time between your heartbeats. A higher variation means your autonomic nervous system is relaxed, recovered, and ready to perform. A lower, suppressed variation means your nervous system is stressed—your body is fighting off lingering fatigue, poor sleep, or impending illness. Today, whether you are wearing a Garmin, an Apple Watch, or a Google Pixel Watch, they all track this baseline metric while you sleep.

When my HRV was unbalanced, it wasn’t just that the power targets were harder to hit. The bigger issue was that I didn’t want to ride my bike. Riding was always my favorite thing to do, but it was starting to feel like a chore. I’d struggle to motivate, and the slightest excuse became a great reason to do something else instead of whatever workout I had scheduled. If I decided to race anyway, I wouldn’t be able to really dig deep in the key moments, and I’d find myself not having much fun as I got dropped.

Then the even bigger problem was the downward spiral. In my 30s, pushing through was a badge of honor. In my 40s, pushing through a suppressed HRV just compounds the problem. Not only can you not perform your best, but the more you push through, the harder things get. You don’t ever have the capacity to recover.

I got to a point where I just thought, this can’t be life. Something has to be wrong if I feel like this. I even went and got checked out by my doctor, but the numbers were all within range. That was when I finally started to pay attention to the metrics I was getting from my smartwatch. Suddenly, HRV wasn’t something abstract; it was very real and very actionable.

That was the turning point. I had to learn to look at my recovery score, swallow my ego, and downgrade a hard interval day to a recovery spin—or take total rest. I learned it takes profound discipline to listen to an algorithm over my own ambition, but preventing that downward spiral is how older riders stay in the game.

In my 30s, my training plan was effectively nonexistent. If I had to sum it up, the strategy was simply: go hard all the time. Every sunny ride was about hunting for a PR, and I used to go on rides where all I did was mash up and down hills as fast as possible. There was a local hill someone bet me I couldn’t climb in under 20 minutes. I used to ride to the base with nothing held back, absolutely empty the tank up the climb, and then head home after a few minutes of breathing hard. I could shrug off anything.

You can get away with that “whatever, whenever, always hard” approach when your body naturally resets overnight. But as you age, it becomes a trap. Trying to hold onto that carefree adrenaline rush of racing whenever you want just isn’t sustainable.…

items.title: ‘I Expected More From Him’: A Lidl-Trek Teammate Says Out Loud What Many Were Thinking About Juan Ayuso
items.author: ahood
items.content: Mathias Vacek had a front-row seat to Juan Ayuso’s struggles in 2026 and opens up about his own classics ambitions at Lidl-Trek.
items.lbText:
Vacek, inset, watched as Ayuso struggled in 2026. (Photo: Getty Images)

Mathias Vacek might not be a household name yet, but he’s a rising star at budding super team Lidl-Trek .

And he clearly isn’t afraid to speak his mind.

In an interview with MARCA , the Czech rider offered a candid assessment of Juan Ayuso’s first season with the team, saying the Spanish star fell short of what he was expecting.

“To be honest, I expected more from him. He started good with the win in the Algarve, and it looked promising, but throughout the season I had the feeling something is missing,” Vacek told MARCA . “He was good, but not at the top like we were used to. I think everyone could see it.”

Ayuso moved to Lidl-Trek in 2026 after a blockbuster transfer and a controversial split with UAE Emirates-XRG. He wanted more freedom, and Lidl-Trek offered him a juicy contract and the chance to headline its grand tour ambitions.

After a hot start to beat Paul Seixas at the Volta ao Algarve , his spring came off the rails. He crashed out of Paris-Nice while in the leader’s jersey and then abandoned Itzulia Basque Country with illness.

Vacek, who made his Tour debut this summer, said he saw warning signs as the Tour approached .

“At the Sierra Nevada training camp, he had allergy problems, he went back home to Andorra, and he started training, but you could feel that something was going on. I don’t know whether it was mental or what,” Vacek said.

“I don’t want to say something I don’t know, but that’s my feeling,” he said. “In the end, at the Tour, you could see he was cooked, and Skjelmose was better than him. Definitely, for me when we signed him, I expected him to be like he was in the earlier years.”

Vacek was also quick to say that Ayuso can fly when everything clicks and stressed he was only sharing his observations, not criticizing his teammate.

“If he’s really good, if he’s on a wave, he can be top, he can also follow Pogi,” he said. “With these guys, when mentally something is wrong, if something wrong or a little detail is missing, they lose the confidence a bit.”

Vacek was equally honest about his own season.

The 24-year-old is emerging as a potential classics powerhouse , but his spring campaign fizzled. He didn’t hit the top 20 all spring and later saved his season with two stage wins and the GC at the ZLM Tour.

What happened? He says he overloaded too soon in an early season build in southern Spain.

“It was a season of ups and downs. Starting at the beginning, the classics went badly for me because I was tired. I started training quite early, and in Spain, with the good weather, you get into shape in three or four weeks,” Vacek told MARCA . “I got carried away with training so early. By the classics, when it really mattered, I was exhausted.”

A reset and an altitude camp helped turn things around. Vacek finished third overall at the Tour de Suisse, then completed his Tour debut by helping teammate Mads Pedersen secure the green jersey.

At the Tour de Suisse, simply staying close to Tadej Pogačar counted for more.

“When I was able to follow Pogačar on a stage of the Tour de Suisse. I think that was something even bigger than a victory for me, because there aren’t many riders capable of following him,” he said. “That was definitely the high point. And the worst moment, without doubt, was the crash in Montréal where I broke my nose.

“That’s cycling. There are always bad moments, but if you know you’re giving everything and committing 100 percent, you know the good moments will eventually come.”

Lidl-Trek brass clearly more upside and Vacek is signed through 2029.

Some see him taking over classics leadership from Pedersen when the big Dane retirees.

“Yes, I’ve had several one-on-one conversations with Mads. He’s a very honest person and tells you things exactly as he feels them,” Vacek told MARCA . “He has told me clearly that I’m one of the riders who will take over when he retires.”

Already four seasons in the WorldTour, Vacek says he’s not a carbon-copy of the marauding Dane, but admits he takes inspiration from the former world champion.

“I want to follow a clear path, try to be like him, and achieve the same victories. I’m a slightly different type of rider because I climb better, but I want to follow in his footsteps,” Vacek said.

“Everything I can learn from him now benefits me. I feel I’m gradually getting closer to his level, so I hope to be there soon if everything goes well.”

He’s obviously already taken one lesson to heart about being a leader — say what you think.

items.title: Cycling’s Lactate Superfuel Has Caused so Much Hype Riders are Sidestepping Sponsors to Get It
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Lactate gels are being sold in 'anonymized' packaging as demand for next-gen fuel used by Pogačar and Tour de France teams explodes.
items.lbText:
Athletes are going off-sponsor to get lactate fuel. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Lactate fueling arrived with such wild hype at the Tour de France that it’s been forced undercover.

ExoLactate has launched an “unbadged” version of its revolutionary gels to meet a surge in demand from athletes who want to tap into the lactate boom, without causing a kerfuffle with team sponsors.

The pioneering Basque brand revealed its exclusive all-silver packaging on Instagram this weekend.

“ExoLactate Gel is used by elite-level athletes to fuel performance at the pinnacle of endurance sports. Sponsorship commitments mean many of these top-ranked ‘testers’ endorse ExoLactate anonymously,” reads the post .

“Now available is ExoLactate Classified, unbranded ExoLactate products, for elite application only.”

The launch of these secretive silver packets is a telling sign.

There’s some serious FOMO around what could be the next superfuel of elite endurance.

The secretive arrival of a first wave of lactate fuels at this summer’s Tour de Franc e was met with a swell of hype, intrigue and suspicion.

Exogenous lactate provides a third fuel source that works alongside the carbohydrates, glucose and fructose, and supercharges metabolism. We wrote a deeper explainer of how lactate fueling works, and why it’s not really “the enemy” here.

Insiders believe lactate fueling has the potential to be as big a breakthrough as the carbohydrate revolution or carbon-plated running super shoes.

But at present, the supply of these next-gen gels and drink mixes is limited.

ExoLactate and Enervit – the partner of Tadej Pogačar ‘s team UAE Emirates-XRG – are leading the boom.

Pogačar was guzzling Enervit’s lactate gel mix en route to his fifth Tour de France title this summer.

ExoLactate was supplying one of the Slovenian’s rival Tour teams, albeit under a strict anonymity clause.

ExoLactate and its “From Lab to Field” research group are also deeply embedded in professional trail running. The gels were used with wild success and podium results at the “Super Bowl” of ultra running, UTMB (Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc).

Meanwhile, the rest of the carbohydrate-focused sport nutrition industry is scrambling to keep up with these lactate first-movers.

At present, only a small handful of derivative, scientifically dubious products are available.

But demand has skyrocketed since the summer.

Approval from Pogačar, proof-of-concept at the biggest bike and trail races in the world, and fear of missing out have made lactate gels a must-have.

ExoLactate founder Aitor Viribay told Velo that he experienced so much interest in his product – a gel that combines 5g lactate and 40g carbohydrate – that it was a no-brainer to launch “Classified.”

The anonymized packaging allows athletes to stray from sponsor commitments, undetected.

No taped-over gels or secretly decanted drink mixes necessary.

“We’ve had so many elites asking for a way to use lactate. And we wanted to support them because we believe in how much potential it has to change performance,” Viribay told Velo .

“But of course elites have their contracts with Maurten or Amacx or Science in Sport or whoever, and we respect that,” he said. “We don’t want to fight with those companies. But the athletes want to use lactate, and they are looking for ways to make it happen.”

Viribay – a former nutritionist at Ineos Grenadiers and the current head of performance at the Solomon running team – said the service honors ExoLactate’s two-way relationship with the elite.

The brand loses revenue and exposure through the service, but gains commitment, feedback, and trust in a fledgling product that’s still evolving.

“There was demand for the service from elites, so we opened the service,” Viribay said. “You have to apply and demonstrate that you have a commitment, and then we can sell to you with that unbranded packaging.

“We don’t make any more money selling the gels this way. These teams and athletes get special discounts,” Viribay continued. “But this is more a service for them because we want to work with them. We are born for elites. We are happy to help them because our goal is not just marketing.”

The professionalization and monetization of pro cycling means every nook and cranny of the sport, and the teams that compete within it, is sponsored.

In the past decades, team partnerships have exploded beyond bikes, helmets, and clothing to include nutrition, leisurewear, recovery products, and even bedding.

Contracts demand athletes “use” – or at least, are seen to be using – products from their team’s invested provider.

But in a sport where the margins are so fine, that’s not always what happens in practice.

Teams commonly ran blacked-out, off-sponsor wheels, saddles, and occasionally bike frames through the 2000s and 2010s. If something was faster, and a team could find a way to use it, they’d make it happen.

A more recent leveling in the bike-tech landscape has made this less of a “thing” in the Pogačar era.

However, off-sponsor pivots remain common in nutrition, where palatability and stomach-compatibility are unique to the individual and essential for success.

And in some cases, products are simply too good to miss.

Maurten’s carbohydrate hydrogels generated so much hype when they helped spark the carbohydrate revolution that the brand foreshadowed ExoLactate by selling unbranded products.

Close to a decade later, Maurten remains a top choice for the sporting elite.

Velo spoke to several WorldTour trainers and nutritionists who are skeptical of products that still lack published research and remain so novel in their use.

Viribay accepted the reluctance when he spoke to Velo . However, he was hopeful that the imminent publication of external studies will persuade the naysayers.

The Basque scientist also suggested the lactate curious more than match the skeptics.…

items.title: Inside the Home Gym of 2 Elite Athletes
items.author: Emily LaPointe
items.content: Haley Smith and Andrew L’Esperance share how they train indoors through a Canadian winter
items.lbText:
If you live in a climate that buries the roads for months at a time, an indoor trainer becomes a major part of preseason training. Just ask Haley Smith and Andrew L’Esperance. The two elite off-road racers—partners on and off the bike—have dialed their indoor setups and workouts for head-of-the-pack performance. At the center of it all are the Wahoo KICKR CORE 2 and the KICKR V6—trainers designed to guide athletes through indoor-to-outdoor transitions with smart features, connectivity, and accessories.

Haley Smith: My indoor workouts are very targeted and optimized: zero junk miles and a high degree of specificity. It’s really common for me to do a large volume of intensity work in a relatively short ride. Torque or muscular endurance work, threshold blocks, and over/unders are frequent indoor rides for me. The KICKR V6 and the ability to toggle between trainer settings on my head unit make it all possible. (Typically, I’m running the ELMNT Roam 3 .) I can adjust the trainer difficulty, turn erg mode on or off, and follow planned workouts right from the head unit without needing to fire up a third-party app. Wahoo plays nicely with third-party platforms, so I’ll often use those for variety and visual stimulus/boredom busters.

Andrew L’Esperance: Either a block of high zone 2, lactic threshold 1 (LT1) work, or a version of over/unders. For the high zone 2 work, I would do 20-to-30-minute blocks and four to eight repeats, depending on the time of year and length of workout. For over/unders, I start with one minute “over” and three minutes “under,” and adjust my recovery time and intensity based on the time of year and goal of the session.

Smith: The KICKR V6 is my favorite indoor training tool—it’s the main event! But a hugely underrated piece of equipment has to be the KICKR Desk . It’s one of those pieces that, before owning, I would have labeled as “nice to have but not necessary.” Now, I am totally dependent on it. Being able to roll the table back and forth and easily adjust the height makes trainer rides so much more enjoyable and practical. No more using a janky bedside table with textbooks stacked to get my laptop at the right height. And the little stabilizing troughs for books or my phone is a nice touch.

L’Esperance: The KICKR CORE 2 —it’s the base of my whole system. During the shoulder and winter seasons, it helps me keep my training consistent, engaging, and effective no matter the weather. The other pieces I can’t live without are the KICKR Desk and KICKR Headwind . I really wasn’t expecting them to be such a key part of the setup, but they certainly enhance the experience. Everything I need is within reach on the desk, and the Headwind offers adjustable cooling during my workouts. I don’t even need to get off the bike.

Smith: All the time! We’re not usually doing the same workout, though the flavor is often the same, but our trainers are set up in the basement on either side of our squat rack. We aim to ride at similar times, which helps with motivation and mobilizing energy to get the work done. It’s nice to have a partner in your suffering, and then we can also provide each other feedback and encouragement on form, effort, etc. We’ll often put the sound system on and turn the basement into a bit of a dance club on the trainers.

L’Esperance: It hasn’t changed significantly since focusing on endurance MTB and gravel events. However, I have refined how I use the indoor trainer. I try to do a maximum of three to four indoor sessions per week throughout the “indoor season.” I keep the sessions structured and focused and make sure the indoor trainer never becomes a grind. In the winter, I’ll also get outside for basic endurance building by running, fat-biking, hiking, and ski-touring. I love moving outside in nature as part of training, and the indoor trainer cannot fully replicate that for me, so that balance is important.

Smith: One of the major differences between XCO MTB, which we used to do, and the longer endurance-style racing we currently do is the steady, uninterrupted pressure on the pedals for extended periods of time. There’s less descending and coasting than there is in XCO, and a lot more constant pedaling at high loads. Indoor training gets rid of things like stoplights and prolonged descents, so we naturally get that steady pressure. It’s not uncommon to have fewer than two to three minutes at less than 100W (that is, fewer than two to three minutes of coasting) in an entire indoor trainer ride. This is both superefficient and very specific to the demands of our racing.

L’Esperance: The endurance off-road racing space is becoming more and more competitive, and starting quite early in the year. Events like BWR AZ, Cape Epic, and Santa Vall are in February and March, so the indoor trainer is an essential race prep tool if you live in a winter climate. The indoor trainer actually allows me to prepare better for these events because of the quality work I can get done.

Located in Atlanta, Georgia, Wahoo Fitness has a vision to be a global leader in smart fitness and training by creating a full ecosystem of software, sensors, devices, data, and performance insights for runners, cyclists, triathletes, and other competitive endurance athletes and fitness enthusiasts. Learn more about Wahoo’s full line of products and apps at WahooFitness.com .

items.title: Velo Poll: Did the UCI Blow It in Schreiber CX Relegation?
items.author: ahood
items.content: Three days later the debate still rages. Did Schreiber deserve to lose the CX European title? You be the jury. Vote in our Velo Poll.
items.lbText:
Marie Schreiber was stunned after she was relegated Saturday. Did the race jury make the right call? (Photo: Billy Ceusters/Getty Images)

Marie Schreiber crossed the line first at Saturday’s European cyclocross championships , but she didn’t win.

The UCI race jury relegated her after citing an irregular sprint, and everyone’s still raging about it.

Check the replay : Schreiber led out the sprint, moved slightly to her left as Lucinda Brand was sprinting beside the barriers.

The race jury didn’t like it and relegated the Luxembourg rider to second, wiping out what would have been her biggest win.

The fallout continues. Brand said she felt beaten straight up and didn’t file a formal protest. Her coach, Sven Nys, questioned the decision as well.

The Luxembourg cycling federation has posted a formal complaint, but so far, Brand is still the official winner.

Was Schreiber closing the door unfairly, or did the jury deliver a punishment that was simply too harsh?

Did the UCI blow it or did they get it right? Vote in our Velo Poll below.

items.title: Garmin’s Latest Update Puts a Real-Time Warning on Drivers’ Dashboards
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: A new integration takes the location data you already share with friends and family and uses it to alert approaching motorists before they even see you.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Today Garmin announced a partnership with the community-driven navigation app Waze. The connection will allow cyclists to show up on a driver’s navigation display, and it all works through the Garmin LiveTrack feature.

If you are unfamiliar, LiveTrack is a free feature built into compatible Garmin bike computers and smartwatches that lets users share their real-time location, speed and course plans with family and friends. It’s a feature that is not unique to Garmin hardware, although competitors have sometimes struggled to execute such a streamlined approach. The Garmin solution allows for a simple list of contacts who get an automatic notification every time you press start on a ride, as well as the option to send links individually.

Garmin is now expanding that usability to Waze. With this new update, that same location data is temporarily broadcast to approaching Waze users as an active icon on their screen. Simply opt in via Garmin Connect and your location will appear as a real-time, moving icon on the Waze mobile app. Drivers in the area who use Waze will see “Live Cycling Alerts” when a rider is using the Garmin integrated feature. Gai Berkovich, vice president and general manager of Waze, said, “By bringing Live Cycling Alerts to Waze, we’re giving drivers a helpful heads-up so they can slow down, stay aware and safely share the road.”

Garmin has also specified that “location sharing is temporary and session-based, and the cyclist’s personal information will not be shared or displayed in Waze.” The feature is now rolling out globally on Android and iOS. Visit the Garmin website for more information.

items.title: Peter Sagan’s Former Team Saved, Another Door Shut for Primož Roglič
items.author: ahood
items.content: Crunch time: TotalEnergies finds a late-hour sponsor, but four other teams are folding in 2026, and no one knows if Primož Roglič will race next year.
items.lbText:
Peter Sagan's final team TotalEnergies will keep racing after the arrival of a new sponsor, but there's no room for Roglič. (Photo: Michael Steele/Getty Images)

TotalEnergies — the second-tier French team where Peter Sagan ended his career — is saved by the bell as teams and riders are getting nervous as 2026 winds down.

Team manager Jean-René Bernaudeau revealed Tuesday that XEFI, a French IT company, committed to three years to keep the long-running team in the peloton.

With just weeks before winter team camps, the announcement went down to the wire to meet registration deadlines and keep riders under contract.

“It’s late, there was pressure, there was anticipation, that much we understand. But today, we savor this feeling of peace and confidence all the more,” sport director Stéphane Heulot told L’Equipe .

Heulot said the team will see a mix of veterans and rising talent for 2027, mostly French, but with more international tilt in the coming season.

Is there room for Primoz Roglič , the superstar Slovenian who is still hunting for a deal? Probably not.

“I would say that today the roster is almost complete. A shock transfer? I don’t know who we could talk about today. Roglič maybe? But honestly, that’s not something we have on the table,” he said. “I don’t want to do a publicity stunt like some teams have done when they don’t actually have the means to hire him.”

The deal saves the team from the edge of oblivion. TotalEnergies confirmed the end of its long-running sponsorship with the team, but appears to be remaining in cycling with partnership with Netcompany-Ineos.

After flirting with international riders like Sagan — who raced his final two seasons with the team — and Edvald Boasson Hagen, the team pivoted back to its French roots the past few years. It won a Tour de France stage in 2024 with Antony Turgis and provided a pipeline for more French riders to start the Tour.

The team was founded in 2000 and has raced the Tour every year since.

Fans will recognize the different names over the years, from Bonjour, Brioches La Boulangère, Bouygues Télécom, Europcar, Direct Énergie, and TotalEnergies, but this has been Bernaudeau’s baby.

The late-hour save is good news for French cycling, which is facing the same problems of rising costs while trying to compete against a few elite super teams at the top of the pyramid.

Coming out of 2026, no major WorldTour teams are facing imminent closure, but there are a few teams in the lower ranks that look to be closing.

France’s St Michel-Auber93 — a modest team from a Parisian suburb that raced a few Tours over the years — is shutting down its long-running men’s that dates back to the 1990s. Management will pivot toward backing the women’s team and hope for a Tour de France Femmes invitation in 2027.

Hitec Products, a women’s Norwegian Continental team, confirmed its shutting down at the end of this season, citing difficulties to get into major races.

Two more second-tier men’s teams that played out-sized roles are also shutting at the end of 2026.

Team Flanders-Baloise, with its DNA dating back to the 1990s, is folding after the Flemish government withdrew key public funding. Long a fixture in the classics, the team was a “talent farm” for budding Belgian riders to make the jump to the WorldTour.

Thomas De Gendt, Sep Vanmarcke, Victor Campenaerts, Oliver Naesen, and Yves Lampaert all did stints with the team over the years.

Kern Pharma, the Spanish ProTeam since 2020, is also restructuring for 2027 after the longtime pharmaceutical company did not extend its sponsorship. Riders like Pablo Castrillo, Roger Adrìa and Raúl García Pierna all raced on the team before bouncing to the WorldTour.

Riders have been told they’re free to find new teams and the squad could continue at a lower level next season.

The Slovenian showed up this week in Taiwan, but there’s still no confirmed team for the four-time Vuelta a España champion.

The 37-year-old parted ways with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe after three season, and it remains uncertain if there will be a closing-hour deal.

Contract talks with several teams, including Visma-Lease a Bike, Unibet Rose Rockets, Pinarello-Q36.5, and Lotto-Intermarché, have all apparently collapsed.

Roglič — once of cycling’s “Big Four” — remains ambivalent about his future and even whether he wants to continue racing.

He still finished second at the Vuelta a España and earned nearly 1,000 UCI points in 2026, which would be valuable to teams chasing a WorldTour license, but a reported $2 million asking price might have to come down if he wants to find a deal this late in the season.

items.title: Room to Go Long: Belgian Waffle Ride Finds Its Ultra in Montana
items.author: Kelly Matkovich
items.content: Sixteen years in the making, BWR’s new 200-plus-mile Brussels Waffle brings the first WUCA North American Gravel Ultra-Distance Championships to Bozeman.
items.lbText:
Riders trace a ribbon of road through Montana’s open ranchlands, dwarfed by the landscape surrounding them. (Photo: ROB WESSELS)

Stella Hobbs had a practical response to the cold and rain at the start of the 2026 Belgian Waffle Ride Montana: make everybody ride harder.

“Between my chattering teeth and numb toes, I decided there was only one solution,” she wrote afterward. “As soon as the neutral ended, I was going to make the race hard. It was time to create some heat.”

The Montana native went to work on the early climbs, taking Cécile Lejeune with her. Across the Gallatin Valley, the weather was conducting several different experiments. Some riders found sunshine. Others rode through passing showers. The moisture settled the dust, the clouds moved across the hills, and the roads kept drawing people farther into a landscape that appeared to have considerably more riding available than we had put on the menu.

Hobbs would win her second consecutive BWR Montana, averaging 20.5 mph across 106 miles. The leading five men averaged more than 22 mph before Hayden Christian claimed a fiercely contested finish. It was the fastest Belgian Waffle Ride we had ever produced. Five riders within a second or two.

For those of us putting it on, Montana was also answering a question we had been asking for years.

For my partners, Phil Tinstman and Randall Coxworth, and me, that question predates our arrival in Bozeman. Belgian Waffle Ride enters its 16th year in 2027, and throughout those years of producing events across North America, we have wanted to create an ultra-distance course.

We have certainly inflicted some substantial days on people. The longest BWR reached 146 miles. Over time, the full-distance Waffle has settled closer to 110 miles, which remains a perfectly respectable distance to spend reconsidering your tire choice.

But the three of us have an affection for going longer. Randall and Phil are Race Across America record holders. I am a Race Across the West record holder. We have spent plenty of time discovering what happens when a ride outlasts your fresh legs, your initial enthusiasm and several entirely reasonable opportunities to stop.

We love that experience. We have wanted to share it through BWR.

At the venues we have been fortunate enough to work with, however, we could never get the ultra course to come together. Creating a worthwhile 200-mile race requires more than dragging a line farther across a map. The terrain has to sustain the adventure. The connections have to work. The extra miles need to earn their place.

In and north of town, the riding opens into broad valleys, rolling ranchlands, gravel climbs and stretches of backcountry that make you curious about what lies beyond the next ridge. From one hillside, you can watch a road work its way across another. A distant group becomes a moving speck. The scale changes your understanding of how much country a bicycle can carry you through.

Under your tires, the experience keeps changing, too. Fast stretches encourage cooperation and occasionally poor judgment. Rougher ground rewards attention. Climbs interrupt conversations that everyone had been enjoying. Pavement connects the pieces, giving riders a chance to find a rhythm before the next change of surface.

This is what we call Unroad: following the character of a place across the surfaces that make it interesting.

Our first two Montana editions gave us the opportunity to build Waffle, Wafer and Wanna courses worthy of that landscape. Going into our third year, we are adding the serving we have been talking about all along.

Named for Belgium’s largest style of waffle, the new 200-plus-mile ultra-distance race will anchor Belgian Waffle Ride Montana , taking place September 17–18, 2027, in Bozeman . It will also host the 2027 WUCA North American Gravel Ultra-Distance Championships , the first official continental gravel ultra-distance championship sanctioned by the World UltraCycling Association .

A Flemish portion with Montana proportions. We suggest arriving hungry.

For Randall, Phil and me, the championship brings together two parts of our cycling lives that we have spent years trying to connect. We get to take the patience, preparation and persistence we love about ultra riding and bring them into a BWR course with room to unfold.

“We’ve always believed a great bike race should ask more of you than how hard you can pedal,” I said when we announced the championship. “Montana gives us the landscape to ask all sorts of decidedly difficult questions.”

Over 200-plus miles, those questions become increasingly personal.

How much effort can you afford on this climb? Have you been eating according to your plan, or waiting for your body to lodge a formal complaint? Can you keep choosing good lines when your hands are tired? Can you let a difficult stretch pass without deciding it represents the remainder of your life?

The distance gives decisions time to accumulate. A restrained first hour can become a gift much later. An unnecessary acceleration can acquire interest. Another rider’s company can change the complexion of an afternoon.

Montana gives those experiences a spectacular setting. The views stretch well beyond the wheel ahead, and the changing terrain keeps you involved in the ride. There is a lot to take in, even when you are busy negotiating with yourself.

The Brussels Waffle will offer continental titles and custom WUCA champion jerseys to the overall male and female winners and to male and female winners in designated age groups. Riders across generations will have the opportunity to chase championship honors, with final eligibility, category rules and membership requirements published alongside the official event information.…
